lessons.title: Understanding the workplace and its resources
lessons.html:
Understanding the workplace and its resources

In this work experience module you apply resource planning and control on a real orchard or vineyard over a production period. The goal is to show that you can get more output, of better quality, from the same or fewer resources. You will keep a portfolio of plans, records and reports, signed off by your workplace mentor.

Step 1: Map the resources

Start by building a clear picture of the section you are responsible for:

  • Blocks: block numbers, cultivars, rootstocks, hectares, tree or vine numbers, age, expected yield.
  • Water: irrigation system per block, pump capacity, allocation, scheduling method.
  • Labour: permanent and seasonal workers, skills matrix, team leaders.
  • Machinery: tractors, sprayers, mowers, platforms; condition and service dates.
  • Inputs: fertiliser and spray programmes, store stock levels.
  • Budget: approved cost per hectare per operation.

Step 2: Find the baseline

Use last season's records to find baseline figures: labour hours per hectare for pruning, thinning and picking; fuel per hectare; water use per hectare; input costs; yield and packout per block. These baselines are what you will try to improve.

Step 3: Identify waste and opportunities

Walk the blocks and observe the work. Look for:

  • Idle time: workers waiting for transport, bins or instructions.
  • Rework: operations redone because of poor quality.
  • Leaks and blocked emitters in irrigation.
  • Uncalibrated sprayers or spreaders.
  • Machines used inefficiently or standing broken.
  • Stock losses, expired products or theft.

List the opportunities and estimate their value in rand or hours. Discuss them with your mentor and choose a few to act on.

lessons.title: Planning and implementing improvements
lessons.html:
Planning and implementing improvements

Choosing improvements

Choose improvements that are practical, affordable and measurable. Good examples:

  • Reorganising picking teams and bin placement to cut waiting time.
  • A sprayer calibration programme at the start of the season and monthly checks.
  • Irrigation maintenance rounds to repair leaks and flush lines, with soil moisture monitoring to adjust scheduling.
  • A tool and PPE control system to reduce losses.
  • Training a team in a skill where productivity or quality is low.
  • Grouping operations by area to reduce tractor travel.

Action plan

ItemExample
ProblemPickers in block 9 wait for bins about 30 minutes a day
ActionDeliver empty bins ahead of teams; second tractor in peak hours
ResourcesTractor and driver for 3 hours per day
ResponsibleForeman and tractor team leader
MeasureBins per picker per day, waiting time
DeadlineStart of week 2 of harvest

Implementing

Explain the change to the team and why it matters. Involve team leaders in the details - they know the practical problems. Start on a small scale if the change is risky, check results after a few days, then expand.

Safety and compliance

Improvements must never reduce safety or break the rules: do not cut re-entry periods, skip PPE or overload workers to save time. Check that changes comply with labels under Act 36 of 1947, water allocations under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, and the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

Evidence

Keep copies of your action plans, briefing notes, job cards and photographs of the work (where the farm allows) in your portfolio.

lessons.title: Measuring results and reporting
lessons.html:
Measuring results and reporting

Measuring the effect

Compare results after the change with the baseline. Use the same measure, the same unit and similar conditions. For example:

  • Bins per picker per day before and after reorganising bin delivery.
  • Water use per hectare and soil moisture readings before and after irrigation maintenance.
  • Spray volume per hectare and coverage checks before and after calibration.
  • Tool losses per month before and after a tool register.

Calculate the benefit in rand where possible. For example, if 40 pickers each pick one extra bin per day for 30 harvest days, that is 1 200 extra bins without extra labour days - work out its value with the farm's cost per bin.

Considering quality

Check that quality did not fall. Faster picking with more damage is not an improvement. Look at packout, rejection rates and quality samples alongside productivity.

Writing the report

Your work experience report should include:

  1. Description of the section and its resources.
  2. Baseline figures and the waste or opportunities you identified.
  3. The improvements chosen and why.
  4. How they were implemented.
  5. Results against baseline, including quality and cost.
  6. Problems encountered and lessons learnt.
  7. Recommendations for the farm.

Use tables and simple graphs. Be honest about improvements that did not work and explain why.

Sustaining improvements

An improvement is only valuable if it lasts. Turn successful changes into standard work instructions, include them in induction and training, and set up regular checks. Agree with your mentor who will maintain them after your work experience ends.

Key points

  • Map resources and establish baselines from records.
  • Look for idle time, rework, leaks, calibration errors and losses.
  • Use action plans with clear measures, responsibilities and deadlines.
  • Never trade safety, compliance or quality for efficiency.
  • Measure against baseline, report honestly and make good changes standard.
